title: Why ‘Harry Potter’ is Fantasy, Not Magical Realism?
use_cases: Use when distinguishing between high fantasy and magical realism genres
Configure when defining world-building rules for hidden magic systems
Implement when auditing literary tropes for urban fantasy narratives
Use when teaching the distinction between academic and commercial genre labels
content:
This is a common point of confusion. Let’s use it to test our rules. The battle of fantasy fiction vs magical realism gets clear here.

Harry Potter has a separate world. Wizards hide from muggles. This means magic is not part of normal, everyday reality. It is a secret, supernatural world. In magical realism, there is only one world. The magic happens right next to the normal.

In Harry Potter, magic is a system. You go to school. You learn spells. You practice. In magical realism, magic just is. No one knows how it works.

In Harry Potter, characters react to magic with wonder or fear. Muggles are terrified of it. In magical realism, characters accept the magic.

So, Harry Potter is clearly fantasy. It is a type called “urban fantasy” because it is hidden within our world. But it is not magical realism. Knowing this really helps you see the line between the genres.

Where did these two types of stories come from? Their histories are very different. This is a big part of comparing fantasy and magical realism.
